title: Popliteal fossa (posterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Long head: ischial tuberosity, with semitendinosus. Short head: linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur.
Lateral side of the head of the fibula, by one tendon for both heads.
Long head: tibial division of the sciatic nerve. Short head: common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (both L5 to S2).
Flexes the leg at the knee and laterally rotates the flexed leg. The long head also extends the thigh at the hip; the short head does not cross the hip.
Ischial tuberosity, with the long head of biceps femoris.
Upper part of the medial surface of the tibia, with sartorius and gracilis (pes anserinus).
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5 to S2).
Extends the thigh at the hip, flexes the leg at the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg.
Posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia.
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5 to S2).
Extends the thigh at the hip, flexes the leg at the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg.
hy: A Baker (popliteal) cyst is a swelling of the bursa between this tendon and the medial head of gastrocnemius. It often connects with the knee joint.

rows: Popliteal surface of the femur, just above the medial condyle.
Posterior surface of the calcaneus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
Plantarflexes the foot at the ankle, most strongly when the knee is straight, and helps flex the leg at the knee.
Lateral surface of the lateral condyle of the femur.
Posterior surface of the calcaneus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
Plantarflexes the foot at the ankle, most strongly when the knee is straight, and helps flex the leg at the knee.
Lower end of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur.
Posterior surface of the calcaneus, by a long thin tendon that usually runs along the medial side of the calcaneal tendon and may blend with it.
Weakly helps gastrocnemius plantarflex the foot and flex the leg at the knee. The muscle is absent in about one limb in ten.
Continues the femoral artery at the adductor hiatus.

Runs down through the popliteal fossa as its deepest structure, against the back of the femur and the capsule of the knee joint; the popliteal vein and the tibial nerve lie closer to the skin. It ends at the lower border of popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
Knee joint, through five genicular arteries, and the nearby muscles: the lower ends of the hamstrings, gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris.
hy: It lies directly against the femur and the knee joint, so it can be torn or blocked by a posterior dislocation of the knee or a fracture of the lower end of the femur. The pulses in the foot are checked after these injuries.
The popliteal artery is the most common site of an aneurysm of a limb artery. It can be felt as a pulsating swelling behind the knee.

rows: Leg, foot and knee joint. It is formed at the lower border of popliteus by the anterior and posterior tibial veins and receives the small saphenous vein.
Runs up through the popliteal fossa between the popliteal artery, which is deeper, and the tibial nerve, which is closer to the skin.
Becomes the femoral vein at the adductor hiatus.
Lateral end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, and the skin and superficial tissues of the lateral side of the foot and the back of the leg.

Passes behind the lateral malleolus and runs up the middle of the back of the calf with the sural nerve. It pierces the deep fascia and passes between the two heads of gastrocnemius into the popliteal fossa.
Popliteal vein, usually. The level at which it ends varies.
Sciatic nerve, as its larger, medial end branch, usually at the top of the popliteal fossa (L4 to S3).

Runs straight down the middle of the popliteal fossa, closer to the skin than the popliteal vessels, and passes under the tendinous arch of soleus. It descends in the back of the leg with the posterior tibial artery, passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.

Muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, popliteus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus; through the plantar nerves, the small muscles of the sole. Skin: the heel and sole; it also gives a root to the sural nerve.
hy: Injury at the knee, as from trauma or a Baker cyst, can weaken plantarflexion, inversion and flexion of the toes and numb the sole. With a complete injury the person cannot stand on tiptoe. Mnemonic TIP: Tibial Inverts and Plantarflexes.
Compression under the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel syndrome) can cause burning pain and numbness of the sole.

rows: Sciatic nerve, as its smaller, lateral end branch, usually at the top of the popliteal fossa (L4 to S2).

Runs along the lateral edge of the popliteal fossa, following the medial border of the tendon of biceps femoris. It winds around the neck of the fibula, just under the skin, and divides there, deep to fibularis longus, into the superficial and deep fibular nerves.

Muscles: the short head of biceps femoris, from its part of the sciatic nerve in the thigh; through its two end branches, the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg and the short extensors of the toes. Skin: upper lateral side of the leg and, through its branches, the lower lateral leg and the dorsum of the foot.
hy: It lies just under the skin against the neck of the fibula, so a fracture there, a tight cast or pressure on the side of the knee can injure it. It is the most often injured nerve of the lower limb.

Injury typically causes foot drop: dorsiflexion and eversion are lost, the foot hangs plantarflexed and inverted, and the knee is lifted high to clear the toes (steppage gait). The lateral leg and the dorsum of the foot are numb. Mnemonic PED: Peroneal (fibular) Everts and Dorsiflexes.
